stem_tex: A stone is thrown straight up from the top of a building with initial velocity 48 ft/sec and hits the ground 5 seconds later. The height of the building, in feet, is Use gravitational acceleration $-32$ ft/sec$^2$.
explanation_tex: With gravity $-32$ ft/sec$^2$, $s(t)=H+48t-16t^2$. Setting $s(5)=0$ yields $H=400-240=160$ feet.

stem_tex: A stone is thrown straight up from the top of a building with initial velocity 48 ft/sec and hits the ground 5 seconds later. The maximum height is reached by the stone after Use gravitational acceleration $-32$ ft/sec$^2$.
explanation_tex: $v(t)=48-32t$ vanishes at $t=48/32=3/2$ seconds; acceleration is negative, so this is the maximum height.

stem_tex: If a car accelerates from 0 to 45 mph in 10 seconds, what distance does it travel in those 10 seconds? (Assume the acceleration is constant and note that 45 mph = 66 ft/sec.)
explanation_tex: Constant acceleration makes average speed $(0+66)/2=33$ ft/sec. Multiply by 10 seconds to obtain $330$ feet.

stem_tex: A stone is thrown at a target so that its velocity is $v(t)=120-20t$ ft/sec, where $t$ is measured in seconds. If the stone hits the target in 1 second, then the distance from the sling to the target is
explanation_tex: Velocity stays positive, so distance is $\int_0^1(120-20t)\,dt=110$ feet.

stem_tex: A stone is thrown straight up from the ground. What should the initial velocity be if you want the stone to reach a height of 144 feet? Use gravitational acceleration $-32$ ft/sec$^2$.
explanation_tex: At the peak, $v=0$. The relation $v^2=v_0^2+2a\Delta s$ gives $v_0^2=64(144)$, hence $v_0=96$ ft/sec.

stem_tex: If the velocity of a car traveling in a straight line at time $t$ is $v(t)$, then the difference in its odometer readings between times $t=a$ and $t=b$ is
choices_tex: the net displacement of the car's position from $t=a$ to $t=b$
the change in the car's position from $t=a$ to $t=b$
explanation_tex: An odometer accumulates distance irrespective of direction, so its change is $\int_a^b|v(t)|\,dt$, not the signed velocity integral.

stem_tex: If an object is moving up and down along the $y$-axis with velocity $v(t)$ and $s'(t)=v(t)$, then it is false that $\displaystyle\int_a^b v(t)\,dt$ gives
choices_tex: the total change in $s(t)$ between $t=a$ and $t=b$
the shift in the object's position from $t=a$ to $t=b$
the total distance covered by the object from $t=a$ to $t=b$
explanation_tex: The Fundamental Theorem gives $\int_a^bv(t)\,dt=s(b)-s(a)$, the signed position change. Total distance instead integrates $|v|$, so D is false in general.

stem_tex:
Which of the following statements characterize(s) the logistic growth of a population whose limiting value is $L$ and whose initial value is less than $\dfrac{L}{2}$?

 I. The growth rate initially increases. II. The growth rate is maximal at population $L/2$. III. The growth rate tends to zero as population tends to $L$.
explanation_tex: For $P'=kP(1-P/L)$, the growth rate is a downward-opening quadratic in $P$, maximized at $L/2$. Starting below $L/2$, it first increases, then decreases to zero as $P\to L$. All three statements hold.

stem_tex: Which of the following differential equations is not logistic?
explanation_tex: Logistic growth contains both a positive linear population term and a negative quadratic term. D is $R'=100-0.2R$, a linear approach-to-equilibrium equation, so it is not logistic.

stem_tex: Suppose $P(t)$ denotes the size of an animal population at time $t$ and its growth is described by the d.e.\ $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.003P(1500-P)$. If the initial population is 300, then the population is growing fastest
explanation_tex: $P'=0.003P(1500-P)$ is maximized at the vertex $P=1500/2=750$. Starting from $300$, the population reaches this value before approaching capacity.
